prompt: How did the Northwest Ordinance of 1787 shape both U.S. westward expansion and constitutional federalism?

options.text: It admitted new western states on equal footing with existing states
It kept western territories as permanent colonies of eastern states
It let the president appoint lifetime governors for every new state
It required new states to adopt unicameral legislatures forever

explanation: Passed under the Articles of Confederation, the Northwest Ordinance created a path to equal statehood while banning slavery there.
fun_fact: The ordinance also guaranteed trial by jury, religious freedom, and public support for schools.

trap_notes.b: The ordinance rejected permanent colonial status in favor of equal statehood.
trap_notes.c: Once admitted, states elected their own governors and legislatures.
trap_notes.d: States drafted their own republican constitutions rather than keeping one set form.
trap_notes.default: The Northwest Ordinance established equal statehood for territories reaching 60,000 residents.

prompt: What constitutional clash emerged when Jefferson and Madison answered the 1798 Alien and Sedition Acts?

options.text: Congress abolished the Supreme Court to protect wartime secrecy
States asserted a right to judge and nullify unconstitutional federal laws
The president vetoed the First Amendment to silence rival newspapers
Federal judges barred all immigrants from voting in state elections

explanation: The Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions argued states could interpose or nullify federal laws, sparking early federalism debates.
fun_fact: The Sedition Act expired in 1801, and Jefferson pardoned those convicted under it.

trap_notes.a: Congress never abolished the Supreme Court, though Federalists passed the Judiciary Act of 1801.
trap_notes.c: The First Amendment was already ratified in 1791 and cannot be vetoed.
trap_notes.d: The Alien Acts lengthened residency for citizenship; they did not come from judicial rulings.
trap_notes.default: The 1798 resolutions pitted state nullification claims against federal sedition prosecutions.

prompt: How did Gibbons v. Ogden (1824) reshape both federal authority and the early U.S. transportation market?

options.text: It allowed states to tax out-of-state steamboats on coastal rivers
It limited federal trade power strictly to overseas shipping
It struck down a state steamboat monopoly under the Commerce Clause
It transferred all canal construction from states to federal courts

explanation: Chief Justice Marshall ruled that federal power over interstate commerce includes navigation and overrides state monopolies.
fun_fact: The ruling opened New York-New Jersey waterways to competing ferry operators.

trap_notes.a: The Court struck down New York's restrictive licensing, not validated state barriers.
trap_notes.b: Marshall defined commerce broadly to include interstate navigation and trade.
trap_notes.d: Courts adjudicate disputes; they do not build or manage canals.
trap_notes.default: Gibbons v. Ogden expanded federal Commerce Clause authority over interstate navigation.

prompt: Why did Lincoln and Congress pursue the Thirteenth Amendment after the 1863 Emancipation Proclamation?

options.text: The Proclamation was a temporary war measure limited to rebel areas
The Proclamation only applied to enslaved people in northern states
The Supreme Court had declared the Proclamation invalid in 1864
Congress wanted to return freedpeople to state-regulated servitude

explanation: Issued under commander-in-chief war powers, the Proclamation left slavery intact in loyal border states until the 13th Amendment.
fun_fact: The Thirteenth Amendment was ratified in December 1865, eight months after Lincoln's death.

trap_notes.b: The Proclamation exempted loyal Union border states and Union-occupied areas.
trap_notes.c: The Supreme Court never struck down the Emancipation Proclamation.
trap_notes.d: The 13th Amendment permanently abolished slavery nationwide, except as punishment for crime.
trap_notes.default: A constitutional amendment was needed to end slavery permanently across the entire nation.

prompt: How did the Fourteenth Amendment's Citizenship Clause overturn the Supreme Court's 1857 Dred Scott ruling?

options.text: It let each state legislature decide who qualified as a U.S. citizen
It restricted citizenship strictly to property-owning taxpayers
It required Congress to approve every naturalization individually
It granted citizenship to all persons born or naturalized in the U.S.

explanation: The Fourteenth Amendment established birthright citizenship and equal protection, nullifying Dred Scott's exclusion of Black Americans.
fun_fact: In United States v. Wong Kim Ark (1898), the Court affirmed birthright citizenship regardless of parents' nationality.

trap_notes.a: The 14th Amendment created a uniform national standard of citizenship, not state-by-state rules.
trap_notes.b: Property qualifications were never part of the 14th Amendment's Citizenship Clause.
trap_notes.c: Congress passes general naturalization laws, not individual approvals for every citizen.
trap_notes.default: The 14th Amendment guaranteed birthright citizenship to everyone born in the United States.

prompt: What administrative shift did the 1883 Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act initiate during the Gilded Age?

options.text: It replaced party patronage jobs with competitive merit-based exams
It required federal agency heads to stand for popular election
It abolished all federal regulatory boards created after 1865
It gave state governors power to appoint federal postal clerks

explanation: Following President Garfield's assassination by a disappointed job-seeker, the Pendleton Act built a professional civil service.
fun_fact: Initially covering 10 percent of federal jobs, merit rules eventually grew to cover most civilian workers.

trap_notes.b: Federal bureaucrats remain appointed, not elected by popular vote.
trap_notes.c: The federal bureaucracy expanded, rather than shrank, after 1883.
trap_notes.d: Federal civil service hiring remained under national, not state, authority.
trap_notes.default: The Pendleton Act replaced the spoils system with merit-based civil service hiring.

prompt: How did the Seventeenth Amendment (1913) reflect Progressive Era goals for the U.S. Senate?

options.text: It allocated Senate seats proportionally by state population
It shifted Senate selection from state legislatures to direct voters
It limited U.S. senators to a single six-year term in office
It ended the vice president's role as presiding Senate officer

explanation: Progressives pushed the 17th Amendment to curb legislative deadlocks and corruption by letting voters elect senators directly.
fun_fact: Oregon pioneered a popular advisory vote for senators in 1904 before the constitutional amendment passed.

trap_notes.a: Each state still receives exactly two senators under Article V.
trap_notes.c: The 17th Amendment did not impose term limits on senators.
trap_notes.d: The vice president remains President of the Senate under Article I.
trap_notes.default: The 17th Amendment established direct popular election of U.S. senators.

prompt: How did World War I mobilization help secure ratification of the Nineteenth Amendment in 1920?

options.text: European allies required U.S. women's suffrage in the peace treaty
Women's wartime labor and civic service weakened anti-suffrage arguments
Congress drafted women into combat units and granted them votes
The Supreme Court ruled male-only voting violated the War Powers Act

explanation: Women's vital wartime roles in factories, nursing, and bond drives helped persuade lawmakers to pass the 19th Amendment.
fun_fact: Tennessee became the decisive 36th state to ratify the 19th Amendment by a single legislative vote.

trap_notes.a: The Treaty of Versailles did not dictate U.S. domestic voting laws.
trap_notes.c: Women served as nurses and clerks, not in combat drafts.
trap_notes.d: Women's suffrage came via constitutional amendment, not a War Powers ruling.
trap_notes.default: Women's wartime contributions strengthened momentum for the 19th Amendment.

prompt: What constitutional shift occurred in 1937 when the Supreme Court upheld New Deal labor and minimum-wage laws?

options.text: The Court ended judicial review over all congressional statutes
The Court banned states from passing workplace safety regulations
The Court broadened economic and Commerce Clause regulatory deference
The Court expanded its membership from nine to fifteen justices

explanation: In West Coast Hotel v. Parrish and NLRB v. Jones & Laughlin Steel, the Court upheld broad federal and state economic regulation.
fun_fact: This 1937 shift helped defeat President Roosevelt's controversial court-packing bill in Congress.

trap_notes.a: Judicial review remained intact; the Court simply applied more deferential scrutiny.
trap_notes.b: The Court upheld Washington State's minimum-wage law in West Coast Hotel.
trap_notes.d: Congress rejected Roosevelt's proposal to expand the Court beyond nine justices.
trap_notes.default: After 1937, the Supreme Court consistently upheld broad federal economic regulation.

prompt: What tension between national security and civil liberties did Korematsu v. United States (1944) expose?

options.text: The Court upheld wartime Japanese American internment under military necessity
The Court struck down Executive Order 9066 as a Fourth Amendment violation
Congress impeached the president for suspending habeas corpus in California
State governors refused to enforce federal wartime rationing rules

explanation: In a 6–3 decision, the Court deferred to military judgment and upheld internment, a ruling later widely repudiated.
fun_fact: In 1988, Congress apologized and paid reparations to Japanese American survivors through the Civil Liberties Act.

trap_notes.b: The Court upheld Korematsu's conviction in 1944 rather than striking down Order 9066.
trap_notes.c: No impeachment occurred over Executive Order 9066.
trap_notes.d: Rationing compliance was not the issue in Korematsu.
trap_notes.default: Korematsu v. United States upheld wartime internment by deferring to executive military claims.

prompt: Why did the Supreme Court block President Truman from seizing U.S. steel mills during the Korean War in 1952?

options.text: The president lacked statutory authority from Congress for domestic seizure
The Tenth Amendment gave steelworkers a right to strike against war orders
Only state governors can operate factories during an undeclared war
The Korean War had already ended before the steel strike began

explanation: In Youngstown Sheet & Tube v. Sawyer, the Court ruled the president cannot seize domestic property without Congress's approval.
fun_fact: Justice Robert Jackson's concurrence created a famous three-tier test for presidential power.

trap_notes.b: The decision rested on separation of powers, not a Tenth Amendment strike right.
trap_notes.c: Governors do not hold exclusive authority over national industrial seizures.
trap_notes.d: The Korean War was ongoing in 1952 when Truman issued his executive order.
trap_notes.default: Youngstown held that the president cannot seize domestic industry without congressional authorization.

prompt: What constitutional principle did United States v. Nixon (1974) affirm during the Watergate scandal?

options.text: Executive privilege is absolute whenever national politics are involved
The president cannot withhold subpoenaed criminal evidence unconditionally
Federal courts lack authority to hear cases involving a sitting president
Only the House Speaker may inspect White House audio recordings

explanation: In an 8–0 ruling, the Supreme Court held that executive privilege is not absolute and must yield to criminal trial subpoenas.
fun_fact: President Nixon released the Watergate tapes and resigned sixteen days after the ruling.

trap_notes.a: The Court recognized executive privilege exists but rejected absolute immunity from criminal subpoenas.
trap_notes.c: The Court asserted judicial authority to decide the scope of executive privilege.
trap_notes.d: The subpoena came from a federal special prosecutor for a criminal trial, not the House Speaker.
trap_notes.default: United States v. Nixon affirmed that no president is above the rule of law.

secondary_geo.label: Federal Reserve Bank of New York

prompt: Why did Congress structure the Federal Reserve as an independent agency accountable to Congress rather than the Treasury?

options.text: To let private banks set federal income tax rates without votes
To insulate monetary policy from short-term election pressures
To prevent states from chartering any local commercial banks
To eliminate congressional oversight of the U.S. money supply

explanation: Long 14-year governor terms and independent funding shield interest-rate decisions from partisan election cycles.
fun_fact: The Federal Reserve Chair still testifies twice yearly before Congress under the Humphrey-Hawkins Act.

trap_notes.a: Income tax rates are set by Congress and the president, never by the Federal Reserve.
trap_notes.c: The U.S. maintains a dual banking system with both state- and federally chartered banks.
trap_notes.d: The Fed was created by Congress and remains subject to statutory oversight.
trap_notes.default: Central bank independence helps keep monetary policy focused on long-term price stability.

prompt: What shared constitutional basis supported both the 1887 Interstate Commerce Act and the 1890 Sherman Antitrust Act?

options.text: The Treaty Power allowing presidents to set domestic rail fares
The Tenth Amendment reserving monopoly policing to city councils
Congress's power to regulate commerce among the several states
The Sixteenth Amendment's grant of federal corporate income taxes

explanation: Congress used its Article I Commerce Clause power to curb railroad rate abuses and monopolistic trusts.
fun_fact: The Interstate Commerce Commission (1887) was the first independent federal regulatory agency.

trap_notes.a: Treaty power governs foreign agreements, not domestic railroad rates.
trap_notes.b: These were federal laws enacted by Congress, not city ordinances.
trap_notes.d: The 16th Amendment was ratified in 1913, over two decades later.
trap_notes.default: Both Gilded Age laws rested on Congress's Interstate Commerce Clause authority.

prompt: How did ratifying the Sixteenth Amendment in 1913 transform U.S. federal revenue policy?

options.text: It replaced state sales taxes with a single national property tax
It barred Congress from collecting tariffs on imported goods
It required a balanced federal budget at the end of every fiscal year
It authorized a federal income tax without apportioning by population

explanation: After Pollock (1895) blocked an unapportioned income tax, the 16th Amendment enabled modern progressive federal income taxation.
fun_fact: Before 1913, tariffs and excise taxes provided nearly all federal government revenue.

trap_notes.a: States retained their own tax systems; there is no national property tax.
trap_notes.b: Congress kept the power to levy tariffs alongside the new income tax.
trap_notes.c: The U.S. Constitution contains no balanced-budget requirement.
trap_notes.default: The 16th Amendment empowered Congress to levy a federal income tax.

prompt: How does the Social Security Act of 1935 illustrate cooperative federalism in the U.S. economy?

options.text: It paired a national old-age pension with state-run unemployment programs
It forced private banks to pay monthly stipends directly to retirees
It ended all federal grants-in-aid to state welfare departments
It transferred authority over military pensions to county governments

explanation: Social Security combined federal old-age insurance with federal-state partnerships for unemployment and public assistance.
fun_fact: In Steward Machine Co. v. Davis (1937), the Supreme Court upheld the Act's federal-state tax-credit design.

trap_notes.b: Social Security is funded by federal payroll taxes, not private bank payouts.
trap_notes.c: The Act greatly expanded federal grants-in-aid to states.
trap_notes.d: Military pensions remained a federal responsibility.
trap_notes.default: The Social Security Act blended national insurance with state-administered safety-net programs.

prompt: In Wickard v. Filburn (1942), why could Congress regulate wheat grown solely for a farmer's own use?

options.text: Aggregate home-grown wheat substantially affects interstate market prices
The Fifth Amendment lets Congress seize any surplus farm grain
Ohio had transferred all agricultural powers to the USDA in 1938
All wheat planted in the Midwest is automatically sold overseas

explanation: The Court held that even local, non-commercial activity can be regulated if its combined national effect shapes interstate commerce.
fun_fact: Roscoe Filburn argued he fed his extra wheat to livestock on his own Ohio farm.

trap_notes.b: The case involved acreage quotas under the Commerce Clause, not Fifth Amendment seizures.
trap_notes.c: Ohio did not surrender its state police powers to the USDA.
trap_notes.d: Filburn's wheat was consumed on his own farm, not exported.
trap_notes.default: Wickard v. Filburn established the aggregation principle under the Commerce Clause.

prompt: What Fifth Amendment debate did Kelo v. City of New London (2005) spark over local economic development?

options.text: Whether cities may seize private homes for a public redevelopment plan
Whether states may print local currency during a municipal recession
Whether Congress may ban local property taxes on small businesses
Whether courts must freeze rents nationwide during urban renewal

explanation: The Court ruled 5–4 that transferring condemned homes to private developers for job growth met the Fifth Amendment's 'public use' rule.
fun_fact: After Kelo, over forty states passed stricter state laws limiting eminent domain for private development.

trap_notes.b: Article I, Section 10 forbids states from coining money.
trap_notes.c: Property taxes are a core state and local revenue source.
trap_notes.d: Kelo concerned eminent domain takings, not rent-control freezes.
trap_notes.default: Kelo v. City of New London tested the limits of eminent domain for economic redevelopment.

prompt: Why do state and local officials frequently criticize 'unfunded mandates' enacted by Congress?

options.text: They force states to spend local tax dollars on federal rules without aid
They require states to lend surplus funds to foreign governments
They prohibit state legislatures from passing annual school budgets
They transfer all state sales tax revenue directly to the Treasury

explanation: Unfunded mandates impose federal regulatory duties on states or cities without providing federal funds to cover compliance costs.
fun_fact: Congress passed the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act in 1995 to require cost estimates on new mandates.

trap_notes.b: States do not conduct foreign lending under federal mandates.
trap_notes.c: States continue to set their own education budgets, though mandates strain them.
trap_notes.d: State sales taxes remain state and local revenue.
trap_notes.default: Unfunded mandates require state compliance with federal standards without matching funding.

prompt: What did Citizens United v. FEC (2010) rule about corporate and union spending in federal elections?

options.text: Independent political spending by corporations is protected speech
Corporations may donate unlimited cash straight to candidates
Federal taxpayers must match every corporate campaign ad dollar
Labor unions are barred from endorsing candidates before primaries

explanation: The Court struck down bans on independent corporate and union electioneering expenditures, fueling the rise of Super PACs.
fun_fact: Direct corporate and union contributions to federal candidates remain prohibited by federal law.

trap_notes.b: Citizens United allowed independent spending, not direct corporate donations to candidates.
trap_notes.c: There is no mandatory taxpayer matching of corporate political ads.
trap_notes.d: The ruling protected both corporate and union independent political speech.
trap_notes.default: Citizens United treated independent corporate and union political spending as First Amendment speech.

prompt: How does the Dormant Commerce Clause protect a unified national market within U.S. federalism?

options.text: It prevents states from enacting protectionist tariffs against other states
It empowers state governors to negotiate bilateral trade pacts abroad
It requires all states to charge identical retail sales tax rates
It bans federal agencies from regulating interstate trucking routes

explanation: Even when Congress is silent, the Dormant Commerce Clause bars states from discriminating against out-of-state goods.
fun_fact: Eliminating state trade wars was a major reason delegates replaced the Articles of Confederation.

trap_notes.b: States are barred from making foreign treaties or trade compacts without Congress's consent.
trap_notes.c: States set their own sales tax rates as long as they do not discriminate against interstate trade.
trap_notes.d: Congress and federal agencies actively regulate interstate transportation.
trap_notes.default: The Dormant Commerce Clause stops states from erecting economic barriers against sister states.

prompt: How did the 1974 Congressional Budget and Impoundment Control Act strengthen Congress's power of the purse?

options.text: It created the CBO and barred presidents from canceling appropriated funds
It transferred authority to print currency from the Treasury to the House
It gave the president a line-item veto over annual defense spending
It ended Senate participation in passing federal tax legislation

explanation: The 1974 Act created the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office and curbed presidential refusal to spend approved funds.
fun_fact: The Supreme Court affirmed in Train v. City of New York (1975) that presidents must spend funds as Congress directed.

trap_notes.b: Currency issuance remained with the Treasury and Federal Reserve.
trap_notes.c: The 1974 Act restricted executive budget power rather than granting a line-item veto.
trap_notes.d: The Senate still votes on and amends all revenue and spending bills.
trap_notes.default: The 1974 Budget Act created the CBO and limited presidential impoundment of funds.

prompt: What sovereignty trade-off do member nations accept when joining the World Trade Organization?

options.text: They adopt a single shared currency managed by Geneva bureaucrats
They submit trade disputes to binding panels that can authorize tariffs
They abolish all national environmental and labor safety standards
They let the WTO collect all domestic corporate income taxes

explanation: WTO members agree to abide by multilateral trade rules and dispute rulings or face retaliatory tariffs.
fun_fact: The WTO replaced the 1947 GATT framework in 1995 to cover goods, services, and intellectual property.

trap_notes.a: WTO members keep their own national currencies.
trap_notes.c: Nations retain domestic regulatory laws, though they must apply them non-discriminatorily.
trap_notes.d: The WTO has no power to levy domestic income taxes.
trap_notes.default: WTO membership subjects national trade policies to international dispute settlement.

prompt: How did Wesberry v. Sanders and Reynolds v. Sims (1964) reshape the geography of U.S. legislative districts?

options.text: They required districts to have roughly equal populations ('one person, one vote')
They mandated that every county receive one seat in each state senate
They banned states from redrawing district maps after a census
They required congressional districts to match state river basins

explanation: The Court struck down malapportioned maps that gave sparsely populated rural counties far more voting weight than cities.
fun_fact: Before 1964, some state senate districts differed in population by more than 100 to 1.

trap_notes.b: Reynolds v. Sims explicitly rejected county-based state senate seats in favor of equal population.
trap_notes.c: States must redraw districts after each ten-year census to maintain equal populations.
trap_notes.d: Districts follow population counts, not physical watersheds.
trap_notes.default: The 1964 reapportionment rulings enforced equal-population legislative districts.

prompt: How do geographic population shifts measured by the decennial U.S. Census alter national political power?

options.text: They change how many U.S. senators each growing state receives
They reapportion the 435 House seats and Electoral College votes
They redraw state borders to keep every state's population equal
They determine how many Supreme Court justices come from each region

explanation: Every ten years, Census counts redistribute the 435 House seats among states, shifting Electoral College totals too.
fun_fact: Faster growth in Sunbelt states like Texas and Florida has shifted House seats south and west.

trap_notes.a: Every state keeps exactly two U.S. senators regardless of population.
trap_notes.c: State borders are fixed and never redrawn for population balance.
trap_notes.d: Supreme Court appointments have no constitutional geographic quota.
trap_notes.default: The decennial Census reapportions U.S. House seats and Electoral College votes among states.

prompt: Why do voters in less-populous states hold greater per-capita weight in the U.S. Electoral College?

options.text: Every state starts with two Senate-based electoral votes regardless of size
Rural counties count twice in federal presidential ballot tallies
Small states receive bonus electoral votes for large land area
Populous states are capped at twenty electoral votes by the Constitution

explanation: Because every state gets at least 1 House seat plus 2 Senate seats, Wyoming has far more electoral votes per resident than California.
fun_fact: No state can have fewer than three electoral votes, the minimum set by Article II.

trap_notes.b: Individual ballots within a state are counted equally, not weighted by county.
trap_notes.c: Land area plays no role in Electoral College allocation.
trap_notes.d: There is no cap per state; California has 54 electoral votes.
trap_notes.default: The two Senate-based electoral votes per state boost small states' per-capita weight.

prompt: What geographic and constitutional issue did the Supreme Court address in Shaw v. Reno (1993)?

options.text: Bizarrely shaped districts drawn predominantly by race face strict scrutiny
States may divide a single city across four different states' delegations
Congressional districts must be drawn as exact geometric squares
Voters in U.S. territories gain voting House seats when maps are redrawn

explanation: North Carolina's narrow, snake-like 12th District triggered Equal Protection review because race appeared the dominant factor.
fun_fact: Traditional redistricting principles include compactness, contiguity, and keeping communities intact.

trap_notes.b: Congressional districts never cross state lines.
trap_notes.c: Districts need not be squares, though irregular shapes can signal gerrymandering.
trap_notes.d: Territories elect non-voting delegates regardless of state redistricting.
trap_notes.default: Shaw v. Reno held that bizarrely shaped districts drawn mainly by race trigger strict scrutiny.

prompt: Under Article I, Section 10, how do western states legally share Colorado River water across state borders?

options.text: Through interstate compacts approved by Congress, like the 1922 Compact
By signing bilateral foreign treaties with the United Nations
Through annual popular referendums held only in downstream cities
By letting each upstream state divert the entire river without consent

explanation: The Compact Clause lets states form binding agreements on shared resources like rivers once Congress gives consent.
fun_fact: Seven states—Colorado, New Mexico, Utah, Wyoming, Arizona, California, and Nevada—signed the 1922 compact.

trap_notes.b: States cannot sign foreign treaties; interstate compacts are domestic agreements.
trap_notes.c: Water allocations are governed by compacts and Supreme Court decrees, not city referendums.
trap_notes.d: Upstream states cannot unilaterally cut off downstream states' equitable share.
trap_notes.default: Interstate compacts with congressional consent govern shared cross-border resources.

prompt: Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, what rights does a coastal state hold in its 200-nautical-mile Exclusive Economic Zone?

options.text: Full authority to ban all foreign commercial ships from passing through
Sovereign rights over fishing, seabed minerals, and energy resources
Total ownership of the airspace for military exclusion zones
Jurisdiction to tax every foreign cargo container crossing the ocean

explanation: In an EEZ, coastal states control marine and seabed resources while preserving freedom of navigation for foreign vessels.
fun_fact: Full territorial sovereignty applies only within 12 nautical miles of a nation's baseline coast.

trap_notes.a: Foreign ships retain freedom of navigation through Exclusive Economic Zones.
trap_notes.c: Sovereign airspace extends only over land and the 12-mile territorial sea.
trap_notes.d: Coastal states cannot tax passing foreign cargo in an EEZ.
trap_notes.default: An EEZ grants resource rights up to 200 nautical miles while keeping seas open to transit.

prompt: Why do western states like Nevada and Utah contain far more federal public land than eastern states?

options.text: Western territories ceded vast ungranted lands to the U.S. upon statehood
The Tenth Amendment forbids eastern states from having national parks
Congress purchased all western farms during the 1930s Dust Bowl
Western state constitutions banned private homeownership before 1900

explanation: Under Article IV's Property Clause, the federal government retained large tracts of public domain in western states.
fun_fact: Roughly 80 percent of Nevada's land area is managed by federal agencies like the BLM and Forest Service.

trap_notes.b: Eastern states host many national parks, such as Acadia and Great Smoky Mountains.
trap_notes.c: Federal land holdings in the West date back to 19th-century territorial acquisitions.
trap_notes.d: Private homesteading and ownership existed alongside federal public lands.
trap_notes.default: Federal public lands in the West stem from territorial acquisitions retained under the Property Clause.

prompt: What jurisdictional principle did Chief Justice Marshall establish in Worcester v. Georgia (1832)?

options.text: Federally recognized tribes are distinct nations exempt from state laws
State governors may dissolve tribal courts inside their state borders
Tribal governments are municipal subdivisions created by county boards
Native American nations must pay state property taxes on reservation land

explanation: Marshall ruled that Georgia laws had no force inside the Cherokee Nation, affirming tribal sovereignty and federal-tribal relations.
fun_fact: Today, 574 federally recognized tribes exercise inherent self-government across the United States.

trap_notes.b: States generally lack authority to dissolve tribal institutions.
trap_notes.c: Tribal sovereignty predates the U.S. Constitution and does not come from counties.
trap_notes.d: Reservation trust land is generally exempt from state property taxation.
trap_notes.default: Worcester v. Georgia affirmed that tribes are distinct political communities free from state control.

prompt: In geographic redistricting, how do 'packing' and 'cracking' work together in partisan gerrymandering?

options.text: Packing concentrates rivals in few districts; cracking splits them across many
Packing adds extra polling places; cracking shortens early voting hours
Packing eliminates rural districts; cracking merges neighboring states
Packing requires paper ballots; cracking mandates electronic voting

explanation: Mapmakers 'pack' opposing voters into a few overwhelming districts and 'crack' remaining voters so they fall short elsewhere.
fun_fact: The term 'gerrymander' originated in 1812 after a salamander-shaped Massachusetts senate district.

trap_notes.b: Packing and cracking refer to district lines, not polling hours or locations.
trap_notes.c: Redistricting never merges states or erases population-based districts.
trap_notes.d: Ballot format has nothing to do with packing or cracking.
trap_notes.default: Packing concentrates rival voters into few seats while cracking disperses them across others.

prompt: How does Europe's Schengen Area alter traditional national border sovereignty among participating states?

options.text: It removes routine internal passport checks while sharing external borders
It merges all member countries into one single unitary nation-state
It abolishes national police forces and replaces them with UN troops
It requires every European resident to hold a Belgian passport

explanation: Schengen nations allow passport-free internal travel while coordinating visa and security rules at external borders.
fun_fact: Named after a Luxembourg border village, Schengen includes 29 European countries.

trap_notes.b: Schengen members remain sovereign states with distinct governments.
trap_notes.c: National police forces continue operating within their own borders.
trap_notes.d: Citizens keep their own national passports.
trap_notes.default: The Schengen Area eliminates routine internal border checks across participating European states.

prompt: Why did federations like the United States, Australia, and Brazil build planned capital districts away from existing major cities?

options.text: To prevent any single state or commercial hub from dominating the federation
To satisfy United Nations rules prohibiting capitals near ocean ports
To ensure federal lawmakers could not be reached by public voters
To place national parliaments outside the country's legal borders

explanation: Neutral federal districts balance regional rivalries—such as North vs. South or Sydney vs. Melbourne—within a federal system.
fun_fact: Ottawa, Canberra, Brasilia, and Washington, D.C. were all selected as geographic compromises.

trap_notes.b: The UN has no rule restricting where countries place their capitals.
trap_notes.c: Planned capitals were built to be accessible national symbols, not isolated from citizens.
trap_notes.d: Federal districts remain sovereign national territory.
trap_notes.default: Planned federal capitals avoid favoring one rival state or dominant metropolis.

prompt: Which idea from John Locke's Two Treatises of Government directly shaped the U.S. Declaration of Independence?

options.text: Monarchs rule by divine right and cannot be replaced by citizens
Governments derive power from consent to protect natural rights
All private property should be owned collectively by parliament
Only hereditary nobles possess the right to petition lawmakers

explanation: Locke argued that people form governments to protect life, liberty, and property, and may alter rulers who break that trust.
fun_fact: Thomas Jefferson echoed Locke's triad as 'Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness.'

trap_notes.a: Locke wrote specifically to refute divine-right absolutism.
trap_notes.c: Locke defended individual property rights as a core natural right.
trap_notes.d: Locke grounded natural rights in all human beings, not hereditary nobles.
trap_notes.default: Locke's social contract theory held that legitimate government rests on consent and natural rights.

prompt: How did Baron de Montesquieu's The Spirit of the Laws (1748) influence the structure of the U.S. Constitution?

options.text: It advocated uniting lawmaking and judging in one supreme council
It urged colonies to adopt direct Athenian voting on every bill
It argued liberty requires dividing legislative, executive, and judicial power
It proposed abolishing written constitutions in favor of royal decrees

explanation: Montesquieu warned that concentrating power in one person or body destroys liberty, inspiring Articles I, II, and III.
fun_fact: James Madison cited 'the celebrated Montesquieu' directly in Federalist No. 47.

trap_notes.a: Montesquieu argued the exact opposite: fusing powers leads to tyranny.
trap_notes.b: Montesquieu favored balanced representative institutions over pure direct democracy.
trap_notes.d: Royal decrees represent concentrated executive power, which Montesquieu opposed.
trap_notes.default: Montesquieu's separation of powers became a cornerstone of the U.S. Constitution.

prompt: Which principle from England's 1215 Magna Carta carried forward into the U.S. Fifth Amendment?

options.text: Universal adult suffrage regardless of property or gender
Abolition of hereditary monarchy in favor of a senate
Separation of church and state in public education
No free person may be deprived of liberty without due process of law

explanation: Magna Carta's Clause 39 bound King John to 'the law of the land,' laying the foundation for constitutional due process.
fun_fact: An original 1215 Magna Carta copy is displayed at the National Archives' sister exhibition in England.

trap_notes.a: Magna Carta protected barons and 'free men,' not universal suffrage.
trap_notes.b: Magna Carta limited the king's power; it did not abolish the monarchy.
trap_notes.c: Magna Carta actually affirmed the freedoms of the English Church.
trap_notes.default: Magna Carta established that the ruler is bound by law and due process.

prompt: How did the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights differ from national bills of rights like the U.S. Bill of Rights?

options.text: It set global aspirational norms for civil, political, and social rights
It created a world police force to arrest local city officials
It replaced every member nation's domestic constitution automatically
It applied only to citizens of the five UN Security Council members

explanation: Chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt, the UN committee drafted a non-binding declaration of universal civil, economic, and social rights.
fun_fact: The UDHR has been translated into more than 500 languages, making it the world's most translated document.

trap_notes.b: The UDHR has no international police force to enforce its articles.
trap_notes.c: It is a non-binding declaration that inspired, rather than replaced, national constitutions.
trap_notes.d: Its rights apply to 'all human beings' everywhere.
trap_notes.default: The 1948 UDHR articulated universal human rights standards across nations.

prompt: What precedent did the 1945–1946 Nuremberg Trials establish for modern international law?

options.text: Individual leaders can be tried for war crimes despite 'following orders'
Sovereign heads of state enjoy permanent immunity for wartime atrocities
Only victorious nations' domestic courts may define genocide
International tribunals can fine governments but never imprison persons

explanation: The Nuremberg Charter rejected the defense of superior orders and held individuals accountable for crimes against humanity.
fun_fact: Nuremberg's principles directly paved the way for the 1948 Genocide Convention and the International Criminal Court.

trap_notes.b: Nuremberg explicitly rejected sovereign immunity for aggressive war and atrocities.
trap_notes.c: The UN Genocide Convention (1948) established an international legal definition.
trap_notes.d: The Nuremberg tribunal sentenced individual defendants to prison and execution.
trap_notes.default: Nuremberg established individual criminal responsibility under international law.

prompt: According to Duverger's Law, why do proportional representation systems produce multiparty coalitions more often than U.S. elections?

options.text: Seats match party vote shares, so smaller parties can win representation
Proportional systems ban any single party from winning over 20 percent
Winner-take-all districts reward third parties with bonus cabinet seats
Proportional systems require voters to rank only two major parties

explanation: When seats are awarded by vote share, minor parties survive instead of being squeezed out as in winner-take-all districts.
fun_fact: Germany's mixed-member proportional system uses a 5 percent national threshold to limit extreme fragmentation.

trap_notes.b: Proportional systems place no upper cap on a popular party's vote share.
trap_notes.c: Single-member plurality ('winner-take-all') districts penalize third parties.
trap_notes.d: Proportional ballots typically offer many competing party lists.
trap_notes.default: Proportional representation lets smaller parties win seats in line with their vote share.

prompt: How does a parliamentary vote of no confidence resolve legislative-executive deadlock differently from a U.S. impeachment?

options.text: It removes a government for lost political support without alleging a crime
It requires a criminal indictment by a supreme court before any vote
It keeps the prime minister in office while dissolving only the courts
It transfers legislative authority permanently to the hereditary monarch

explanation: In parliamentary systems, the cabinet depends on legislative confidence; losing a confidence vote forces resignation or new elections.
fun_fact: U.S. impeachment requires 'Treason, Bribery, or other high Crimes and Misdemeanors,' not mere policy disagreement.

trap_notes.b: A no-confidence vote is a political test in parliament, not a criminal trial.
trap_notes.c: Courts remain independent; a lost vote ousts the cabinet or triggers parliamentary elections.
trap_notes.d: In constitutional monarchies, the monarch acts on ministerial advice and does not take over lawmaking.
trap_notes.default: A vote of no confidence removes a parliamentary government on political, not criminal, grounds.

prompt: How did India's 1950 Constitution blend British parliamentary traditions with U.S. constitutional features?

options.text: It paired a Westminster cabinet system with a written charter and judicial review
It kept the British monarch as India's permanent head of state
It replaced India's parliament with an appointed council of governors
It banned political parties from competing in state-level elections

explanation: India adopted a prime minister and cabinet from Britain alongside an entrenched bill of Fundamental Rights and an independent Supreme Court.
fun_fact: India's Constitution is the longest written national constitution in the world.

trap_notes.b: India became a republic in 1950 with an indirectly elected president as head of state.
trap_notes.c: India established a directly elected lower house (Lok Sabha) with universal suffrage.
trap_notes.d: India has a vibrant multiparty system at both national and state levels.
trap_notes.default: India's Constitution combined parliamentary cabinet government with written rights and judicial review.

prompt: How did the 1998 Good Friday Agreement use power-sharing to end decades of conflict in Northern Ireland?

options.text: It required unionist and nationalist parties to govern together in the executive
It banned all political parties from campaigning on constitutional issues
It partitioned Belfast into two separate UN-administered city-states
It eliminated local assemblies in favor of direct rule from London

explanation: The agreement created a consociational assembly where both unionist and nationalist blocs share executive leadership and mutual vetoes.
fun_fact: Voters in both Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland approved the accord by referendum in May 1998.

trap_notes.b: Parties remained free to advocate peacefully for union or Irish unity.
trap_notes.c: Belfast remained a single city governed under Northern Ireland's devolved assembly.
trap_notes.d: The accord ended direct rule by restoring a devolved Northern Ireland Assembly.
trap_notes.default: The Good Friday Agreement established mandatory cross-community power-sharing.

prompt: What core principle of modern international relations emerged from the 1648 Peace of Westphalia?

options.text: Each sovereign state holds exclusive authority within its own borders
A European parliament may veto tax laws passed by member kingdoms
Religious minorities must migrate to a single neutral island state
All European armies were merged under one permanent papal command

explanation: Ending the Thirty Years' War, Westphalia recognized territorial sovereignty and non-interference in domestic affairs.
fun_fact: Even today, the UN Charter's Article 2 echoes Westphalian sovereign equality of states.

trap_notes.b: No European parliament existed in 1648.
trap_notes.c: The treaties granted limited religious toleration within states rather than mass exile.
trap_notes.d: Westphalia actually weakened supranational imperial and papal claims over states.
trap_notes.default: The Peace of Westphalia anchored the modern system of sovereign territorial states.

prompt: How did South Africa's 1996 Constitution and Truth and Reconciliation Commission aid its transition from apartheid?

options.text: They combined an enforceable Bill of Rights with public testimony for healing
They barred the new Constitutional Court from reviewing parliamentary laws
They restricted voting to citizens who had held office before 1990
They abolished all nine provincial governments to centralize power

explanation: South Africa replaced parliamentary supremacy with constitutional supremacy while the TRC documented past abuses to foster reconciliation.
fun_fact: South Africa's 1996 Bill of Rights protects civil liberties alongside rights to housing, healthcare, and education.

trap_notes.b: The Constitutional Court was specifically empowered to strike down unconstitutional laws.
trap_notes.c: The 1994 election introduced universal adult suffrage for all South Africans.
trap_notes.d: The 1996 Constitution created nine provinces with shared powers.
trap_notes.default: South Africa paired a rights-protecting constitution with the Truth and Reconciliation Commission.

prompt: Which agent of political socialization typically exerts the earliest and strongest influence on a person's core party identity?

options.text: The family, through everyday discussions and shared values at home
Federal regulatory agencies, through annual tax-filing forms
Appellate courts, through published constitutional opinions
Foreign embassies, through international cultural exchanges

explanation: Political science research consistently shows that parents and family life shape early political attitudes and party leanings.
fun_fact: Schools, peer groups, religious communities, and media also shape civic attitudes over a lifetime.

trap_notes.b: Tax forms do not socialize children into partisan or civic identities.
trap_notes.c: Most citizens rarely read appellate court opinions during childhood.
trap_notes.d: Foreign embassies have minimal direct contact with young domestic citizens.
trap_notes.default: The family is the primary early agent of political socialization.

prompt: In U.S. policymaking, which three actors form an 'iron triangle'?

options.text: The president, the Supreme Court, and state governors
Congressional committees, executive agencies, and interest groups
Political parties, television networks, and polling firms
City mayors, county sheriffs, and local school boards

explanation: An iron triangle is a stable, mutually supportive alliance among a legislative committee, a bureaucratic agency, and an interest group.
fun_fact: Broader, looser coalitions of experts and activists are often called 'issue networks.'

trap_notes.a: The Supreme Court and governors are outside federal sub-government iron triangles.
trap_notes.c: Media and pollsters influence public opinion rather than forming a regulatory triangle.
trap_notes.d: Local officials operate at the municipal level, not inside federal agency triangles.
trap_notes.default: An iron triangle links congressional committees, bureaucratic agencies, and interest groups.

prompt: How do large interest groups overcome the 'free-rider problem' when recruiting dues-paying members?

options.text: By asking federal judges to fine non-members for ignoring petitions
By restricting public policy benefits strictly to paid donors
By offering selective benefits like discounts or magazines to members
By barring non-members from voting in state and local elections

explanation: Because everyone enjoys public goods like clean air, groups offer exclusive perks—selective benefits—to motivate membership.
fun_fact: Economist Mancur Olson analyzed this collective-action dilemma in The Logic of Collective Action (1965).

trap_notes.a: Interest groups are private associations with no power to fine non-members.
trap_notes.b: Collective goods like cleaner air or lower taxes cannot be withheld from non-members.
trap_notes.d: Private groups cannot restrict citizens' constitutional voting rights.
trap_notes.default: Selective material benefits encourage people to join rather than free-ride.

prompt: What is the 'agenda-setting' effect of news media in democratic politics?

options.text: Media coverage shapes which issues the public sees as most important
News anchors cast tie-breaking votes in congressional committees
Reporters draft the official party platforms at national conventions
Television networks decide which citizens qualify for jury duty

explanation: By choosing which stories to highlight, news outlets influence what issues voters and lawmakers prioritize.
fun_fact: Scholars Maxwell McCombs and Donald Shaw coined agenda-setting theory during the 1968 U.S. election.

trap_notes.b: Journalists have no legislative voting power.
trap_notes.c: Party delegates and committees write party platforms, not reporters.
trap_notes.d: Court clerks select jury pools from voter and driver records.
trap_notes.default: Agenda-setting means media coverage influences what issues the public thinks about.

prompt: Why does a scientific public-opinion poll rely on random sampling of about 1,000 respondents?

options.text: Random selection ensures every adult has an equal chance to be included
Federal law prohibits pollsters from surveying more than 1,000 people
A 1,000-person sample eliminates all sampling error completely
Random sampling guarantees every respondent shares the same party

explanation: Random probability sampling lets a modest sample represent a large nation within a known margin of error.
fun_fact: George Gallup famously beat the huge but biased 1936 Literary Digest straw poll using scientific sampling.

trap_notes.b: There is no legal cap on survey sample size; 1,000 balances cost and precision.
trap_notes.c: Every sample retains a margin of error (often around plus or minus 3 percentage points).
trap_notes.d: A good random sample reflects diverse partisan views rather than one party.
trap_notes.default: Random sampling gives every population member an equal chance of selection.

prompt: Which pair accurately distinguishes a legal civic duty from a voluntary civic responsibility in the United States?

options.text: Voting is legally required; obeying traffic laws is voluntary
Serving on a jury is legally required; voting in elections is voluntary
Attending town halls is legally required; paying taxes is voluntary
Running for office is legally required; jury duty is voluntary

explanation: Civic duties like jury service, obeying laws, and paying taxes are required by law; voting and volunteering are civic responsibilities.
fun_fact: Unlike the United States, countries such as Australia and Belgium enforce compulsory voting.

trap_notes.a: Obeying laws is mandatory, whereas voting is voluntary in the U.S.
trap_notes.c: Paying taxes is a legal duty; attending town halls is voluntary.
trap_notes.d: Jury duty is legally required when summoned; running for office is voluntary.
trap_notes.default: Jury service is a mandatory civic duty, while voting is a voluntary responsibility.

prompt: Which requirement is generally part of the U.S. naturalization process for adult permanent residents?

options.text: Owning real estate in the state where the applicant resides
Securing a personal sponsorship vote from two U.S. senators
Demonstrating basic English and U.S. civics knowledge plus residency
Serving at least four years in the armed forces before applying

explanation: Naturalization applicants typically show lawful permanent residence, good moral character, English proficiency, and civics knowledge.
fun_fact: The process concludes with taking the Oath of Allegiance at a naturalization ceremony.

trap_notes.a: Property ownership has no place in U.S. naturalization requirements.
trap_notes.b: USCIS administers naturalization under federal law without Senate sponsorship.
trap_notes.d: Military service can speed up naturalization, but it is not required.
trap_notes.default: Naturalization requires lawful residency, good character, and passing English and civics tests.

prompt: How does cooperative ('marble cake') federalism differ from dual ('layer cake') federalism?

options.text: Federal and state governments share overlapping policy and funding roles
State governments are abolished so Congress can run local schools
Federal and state powers remain strictly separated into airtight spheres
Only municipal mayors are permitted to collect income and sales taxes

explanation: In cooperative federalism, national, state, and local governments collaborate on highways, healthcare, and education through grants.
fun_fact: Political scientist Morton Grodzins coined the 'marble cake' metaphor in the 1960s.

trap_notes.b: Cooperative federalism preserves state governments as active partners.
trap_notes.c: Strict separation describes dual ('layer cake') federalism, not cooperative federalism.
trap_notes.d: Taxing power is shared across federal, state, and local governments.
trap_notes.default: Cooperative federalism features shared, overlapping responsibilities across government levels.

prompt: Under Dillon's Rule, what legal relationship exists between a state government and its cities or counties?

options.text: Cities hold independent sovereignty equal to that of the state
Local governments exercise only powers expressly granted by the state
Counties may veto state tax laws that affect local businesses
Municipal charters are protected by the U.S. Tenth Amendment

explanation: Named after Iowa Judge John Dillon, Dillon's Rule treats local governments as creatures of the state with narrow delegated powers.
fun_fact: Many states soften Dillon's Rule by granting larger cities 'home rule' charters.

trap_notes.a: Unlike states in the federal system, cities lack inherent constitutional sovereignty.
trap_notes.c: Counties cannot veto state statutes.
trap_notes.d: The Tenth Amendment reserves powers to the states, not specifically to municipalities.
trap_notes.default: Dillon's Rule holds that local governments have only the powers granted by the state.

prompt: How does the council-manager form of city government operate?

options.text: An elected mayor appoints all city council members and judges
A state governor directly runs the city's police and fire agencies
An elected council hires a professional city manager to run operations
Citizens vote in weekly town meetings to approve every city invoice

explanation: In a council-manager system, the elected council sets policy and hires a nonpartisan manager to oversee daily administration.
fun_fact: Staunton, Virginia, appointed the nation's first city manager in 1908 during the Progressive Era.

trap_notes.a: Voters elect the city council; the mayor does not appoint council members.
trap_notes.b: Municipal administration remains local rather than run by the governor.
trap_notes.d: Day-to-day administration is delegated to the hired manager, not weekly votes.
trap_notes.default: Council-manager cities pair an elected policy council with an appointed professional manager.

prompt: How does the standard of proof in a U.S. criminal trial differ from most civil lawsuits?

options.text: Criminal trials require preponderance of evidence; civil suits require certainty
Both criminal and civil trials require unanimous proof beyond a doubt
Civil trials require no evidence if a plaintiff hires a licensed attorney
Criminal trials require proof beyond a reasonable doubt; civil uses preponderance

explanation: Because liberty is at stake, criminal prosecutors must prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, while civil cases usually use preponderance.
fun_fact: Preponderance of the evidence simply means a claim is more likely true than not (over 50 percent).

trap_notes.a: This reverses the standards: criminal cases demand the highest burden of proof.
trap_notes.b: Most civil lawsuits use the lower preponderance-of-the-evidence standard.
trap_notes.c: Civil plaintiffs must still present evidence meeting the legal burden of proof.
trap_notes.default: Criminal trials require proof beyond a reasonable doubt, higher than civil preponderance.

prompt: What happens when a criminal defendant accepts a plea bargain in a U.S. court?

options.text: The defendant pleads guilty to a lesser charge or sentence to avoid trial
The jury sets the defendant's sentence before hearing any witness testimony
The prosecutor drops all charges in exchange for a civil fine paid to police
The judge transfers the case straight to the U.S. Supreme Court

explanation: In a plea bargain, the defendant waives a jury trial and pleads guilty in exchange for reduced charges or a lighter sentence.
fun_fact: More than 90 percent of federal and state criminal convictions result from guilty pleas rather than trials.

trap_notes.b: A plea bargain avoids a jury trial altogether.
trap_notes.c: Plea bargains result in a criminal conviction on the agreed charge, not dropped charges.
trap_notes.d: Trial courts approve plea agreements; cases do not jump to the Supreme Court.
trap_notes.default: Plea bargaining trades a guilty plea for reduced charges or a lighter recommended sentence.

prompt: Under Article III, in which type of dispute does the U.S. Supreme Court hold original jurisdiction?

options.text: Appeals from state traffic courts challenging local parking fines
Lawsuits between two or more U.S. states or involving foreign ambassadors
Federal felony prosecutions initiated by a U.S. Attorney's office
Divorce and probate disputes involving residents of the District of Columbia

explanation: Article III, Section 2 gives the Supreme Court original jurisdiction in cases affecting ambassadors and disputes between states.
fun_fact: Most Supreme Court cases arrive via appellate jurisdiction rather than original jurisdiction.

trap_notes.a: Local traffic disputes are heard first in state or municipal courts.
trap_notes.c: Federal felony trials begin in U.S. District Courts, not the Supreme Court.
trap_notes.d: Family and probate cases are handled by local trial courts.
trap_notes.default: The Supreme Court's original jurisdiction covers state-versus-state and ambassador cases.

prompt: What has the Supreme Court accomplished through the doctrine of 'selective incorporation'?

options.text: It allowed states to opt out of federal taxes by passing local bills
It merged all federal circuit courts into one national appellate panel
It applied most Bill of Rights protections to state governments case by case
It granted automatic U.S. citizenship to residents of new territories

explanation: Using the 14th Amendment's Due Process Clause, the Court gradually made key Bill of Rights guarantees binding on the states.
fun_fact: Gitlow v. New York (1925) began modern selective incorporation with free speech and press.

trap_notes.a: Selective incorporation concerns civil liberties, not tax opt-outs.
trap_notes.b: Federal courts remain organized into regional circuits and district courts.
trap_notes.d: Territorial citizenship is governed by federal statutes and the Insular Cases.
trap_notes.default: Selective incorporation applies fundamental Bill of Rights protections to state governments.

prompt: In Buckley v. Valeo (1976), what distinction did the Supreme Court draw in federal campaign finance law?

options.text: Congress may cap direct donations to candidates, not candidates' own spending
Congress may ban all television campaign ads sixty days before an election
Candidates must fund their entire campaigns solely from small cash gifts
Political parties may not endorse candidates running for the U.S. Senate

explanation: The Court upheld contribution limits to prevent corruption, but struck down spending caps as unconstitutional limits on speech.
fun_fact: Buckley v. Valeo established the framework for modern federal campaign finance jurisprudence.

trap_notes.b: Blanket bans on campaign ads violate First Amendment political speech protections.
trap_notes.c: Candidates may spend unlimited amounts of their own personal funds.
trap_notes.d: Political parties enjoy broad First Amendment rights to endorse candidates.
trap_notes.default: Buckley v. Valeo allowed contribution limits while protecting campaign spending as speech.
